messages.content: I want to develop knowledge editing that propagates temporally scoped factual changes through multi-hop reasoning without overwriting valid historical knowledge. What does that goal require?

The edit must affect more than a direct question about the changed fact. When a question requires several reasoning steps and one of those steps depends on the edited fact, the answer should reflect the change for the relevant time period. At the same time, an earlier fact that remains true for its historical period must still be available rather than being replaced by a timeless version of the new fact.
So propagation does not mean making the new fact apply everywhere?

Right. Propagation concerns the implications of the change wherever that change is temporally applicable. If a question concerns an earlier period in which a different fact was valid, preserving that historical fact is part of the goal. The system needs to reason with the time scope of the fact, not merely repeat whichever version was edited most recently.
And what makes the reasoning multi-hop here?

A multi-hop question needs more than direct retrieval of the edited fact. It requires connecting that fact with one or more other pieces of information to reach an answer. The relevant challenge is that the temporal qualification must carry through those connections: a fact applicable during one period should influence a chain of reasoning about that period, but not an otherwise similar chain about a period when the fact did not apply.
Would getting direct questions about the edited fact right be enough?

No. Direct recall alone would not establish the stated goal. The explicit performance requirement is at least 90% accuracy on held-out multi-hop questions requiring temporally scoped edited facts. Those questions must actually require reasoning through the edited information; otherwise, they would not test the propagation the goal calls for.
What is the significance of “held-out” in that requirement?

It means the accuracy target is for questions reserved for evaluation rather than the questions used to shape the edit. The requirement is not just to produce the edited fact on familiar prompts, but to answer held-out, multi-hop questions that depend on that fact and its time scope. The goal states the threshold—at least 90%—but does not report that the threshold has been reached.
I also want to be clear about what must not be damaged by the editing.

Valid historical knowledge must remain intact, and unrelated factual knowledge must not be substantially disrupted. The stated accuracy constraint is to keep historical and unrelated factual accuracy within one percentage point of the unedited model. That comparison is against the unedited model, not against the accuracy on the temporally scoped, edited multi-hop questions.
Is one percentage point the same as a one-percent relative change?

No. A percentage-point difference compares accuracy rates directly; a relative percent change scales the difference by the original rate. The requirement specifically says within one percentage point of the unedited model. It does not give the unedited model’s accuracy value, so there is no particular baseline score to insert into that comparison.
Does preserving historical accuracy just mean the model should be able to mention an old fact if asked for it?

It includes being able to answer accurately about the historical period, but the larger point is that the old fact must retain its proper scope in reasoning. If a question depends on what was true at an earlier time, the edit should not cause an answer based on a later change to displace that historically valid answer. Historical preservation matters alongside the multi-hop propagation of the edited fact.
Then there are two ways the goal could fail even if an edit seems to work locally?

Yes. The edited fact might be available for a direct question yet fail to influence a held-out multi-hop answer that requires it. Or it might influence answers too broadly, overwriting valid historical knowledge or disturbing unrelated facts. The goal asks for both appropriate propagation and restraint, with the two stated accuracy requirements providing separate checks on those aspects.
How should I read “unrelated” in the preservation requirement?

It refers to factual knowledge outside the change being edited and the reasoning that properly depends on it. The edit is not meant to create broad changes to answers that have no relevant connection to the temporally scoped fact. The node does not specify particular unrelated topics; it sets an accuracy comparison for unrelated factual knowledge against the unedited model.
Could we describe the intended behavior without committing to a particular editing technique?

Yes. The intended behavior is that a factual change is represented with its applicable time scope, used in multi-hop reasoning when a question calls for it, and kept from erasing historically valid information or degrading unrelated factual answers. That description states the goal without presuming an implementation or claiming that an experiment has demonstrated it.
I want the targets stated together, since a high edited-question score alone would be misleading.

The targets are: at least 90% accuracy on held-out multi-hop questions requiring temporally scoped edited facts, while keeping historical and unrelated factual accuracy within one percentage point of the unedited model. Meeting the first target without the preservation constraint would not satisfy the full goal, and preserving prior accuracy without propagating the applicable edit through multi-hop reasoning would not satisfy it either.
So the edit has to be consequential when its time condition applies, but not become an unconditional replacement for the past?

Exactly. The factual change should matter throughout a relevant chain of reasoning for its applicable time period. It should not turn a time-bound change into a claim that the same fact was always true, nor should it overwrite knowledge that remains valid for an earlier period. That is the distinction the goal is trying to maintain.
And these are desired outcomes, not results we already have?
Yes. The statement defines a development goal and two performance requirements. It does not provide measured accuracy, a completed method, or evidence that either threshold has been achieved.

For the temporally scoped editing goal, I’m proposing that we attach interval-indexed fact patches to a frozen model, then gate time-filtered multi-hop retrieval by edited entities while retaining historical versions. Can you unpack that?

The proposal keeps the model itself frozen and attaches fact patches that are indexed by the time intervals in which their contents apply. When a question calls for multi-hop reasoning, retrieval would be filtered by the relevant time and gated by whether an edited entity is involved. Historical versions would remain available, so a patch applicable to one interval would not simply erase a fact that remains valid for another.
What does “patch” imply here? Is it a change to the model’s parameters?

Not in this proposal. A patch is an attached factual change, while the model remains frozen. The distinction matters because the proposed route is to make the changed information available to reasoning through the patches and retrieval, rather than describing a change to the model’s underlying parameters. The proposal does not specify a particular format for those patches.
And the intervals are there so a patch is not treated as timeless?

Yes. Interval indexing associates a fact patch with the period for which it applies. A question’s temporal scope can then affect which factual version is relevant. Without that qualification, a newly attached fact could be applied to reasoning about a period when a different historical version was valid.
I want the historical versions retained, not just a record that they once existed.

That is consistent with the proposal. Retaining historical versions means they remain usable when reasoning about their applicable periods. The patch adds a time-scoped factual version; it is not presented as an instruction to discard earlier versions that are still historically valid.
How do edited entities enter into the retrieval part?

They provide the gate for retrieval involving the patches. In broad terms, if the reasoning requires information about an edited entity, the retrieval process can bring the relevant time-filtered factual version into a multi-hop chain. The wording does not prescribe an exact test for recognizing an edited entity or a particular retrieval algorithm; it identifies what retrieval is gated by.
Does that mean the edited entity has to appear literally in the question?

The proposal does not impose that condition. A multi-hop question can reach a relevant entity through reasoning rather than naming it at the outset. What matters to the proposal is that retrieval is gated by edited entities as the reasoning proceeds, while the time filter determines which version is applicable. The precise way to implement that gate remains unspecified.
Why describe the retrieval as multi-hop rather than just looking up a patch once?

Because the edited fact may be one link in a chain needed to answer a question. Retrieving a patch for a direct question would not, by itself, make the fact available at the appropriate point in a longer chain. The proposal places time-filtered retrieval in that multi-hop setting so the applicable edited fact can inform reasoning that depends on it.
Could time filtering and entity gating be thought of as separate checks?

Conceptually, yes. Entity gating addresses whether an edited entity is relevant to the reasoning; time filtering addresses which factual version applies to the time at issue. Both matter: an entity match alone does not settle whether a patch is valid for the question’s period, and a time interval alone does not establish that the edited entity belongs in the reasoning chain. That describes their roles, not a mandated order of operations.
Suppose a question concerns an earlier interval. Would the patch necessarily be retrieved anyway?

No such unconditional retrieval is part of the proposal. The time filter is meant to distinguish the applicable version for the period in question. If the relevant fact for that earlier interval is a retained historical version, the proposal calls for that version to remain available rather than having an inapplicable patch overwrite it.
And if the question’s answer depends on several links, the temporal distinction still needs to hold at the edited link?

Exactly. Multi-hop reasoning should not strip away the time qualification when it reaches an edited entity. The retrieved factual version at that link needs to fit the relevant interval, so subsequent reasoning uses a fact appropriate to the question’s time scope. That is how the proposed retrieval approach connects propagation with preservation of historical versions.
I don’t want to imply that keeping the model frozen alone guarantees historical accuracy.

It does not. Freezing the model specifies where the edit is not made—its parameters—but it does not by itself determine which version retrieval supplies or how that version is used in reasoning. The interval-indexed patches, time filtering, entity gate, and retention of historical versions are the other parts of the proposed approach. The proposal does not claim that these parts have already delivered a measured outcome.
Is retaining historical versions different from ignoring the edited fact on historical questions?

Yes. The distinction is about applicability, not a blanket rule to ignore edits whenever a question mentions the past. A patch can itself be relevant to a past interval if that is the interval it covers. Retaining historical versions means the appropriate version remains available for each applicable period, rather than treating one edited version as universally valid or universally irrelevant to historical questions.
Would it be accurate to say the attached patches coexist with the historical versions?

Yes. Coexistence captures the proposal well: interval-indexed patches are attached to the frozen model, and historical versions are retained. Time-filtered retrieval is what makes their different scopes meaningful during multi-hop reasoning. Coexistence alone would not specify how to choose between them, which is why the temporal filter is part of the proposal.
What does the proposal leave open?

It leaves the exact representation of patches, the mechanics of the edited-entity gate, and the retrieval procedure unspecified. It also states an approach rather than reporting an implementation or results. Its concrete commitments are the frozen model, attached interval-indexed fact patches, time-filtered multi-hop retrieval gated by edited entities, and retention of historical versions.
So the intended effect is that the relevant edited fact can travel through a reasoning chain, while an earlier valid fact remains usable in a chain about its own interval?

That is the intended distinction. The proposal supplies time-scoped patches for edited facts and uses entity-gated, time-filtered retrieval to bring an applicable version into multi-hop reasoning. Keeping historical versions available is what prevents the attached change from being treated as a wholesale replacement of valid earlier knowledge.
How can interval-indexed retrieval reject multi-hop paths with incompatible validity windows without suppressing valid historical paths?

A useful conceptual distinction is between a path that cannot be valid for the time the question asks about and a path that is valid for a different, historical time. Interval indexing can help test whether the facts used in a path are temporally compatible with the question and with one another. A path that fails that test should not supply the answer to that question; its historical facts need not be removed from retrieval altogether. That describes a possible way to reason about the issue, not a specified retrieval algorithm.
What would make the windows incompatible?

If two hops are supposed to describe the same point or period, but their validity windows have no time in common, they cannot jointly support that same-time chain. Likewise, a hop whose window does not cover the time required by the question should not be treated as applicable to that time. The important qualification is “supposed to describe the same time”: different windows are not automatically contradictory if the question connects events or facts from different periods.
So checking whether every interval in a path overlaps every other interval could be too aggressive?

Yes. A blanket intersection across an entire path assumes all its facts must hold simultaneously. Some multi-hop questions may instead ask how something at one time relates to something at another. In that case, nonoverlapping windows could be exactly what a valid historical path contains. The test has to respect the temporal relationships required by the question, rather than treating any difference in dates as grounds for rejection.
Can you give a general illustration without assuming a particular edited fact?

Imagine two versions of a fact about an entity: one valid in an earlier interval and another valid in a later interval. A question explicitly about the earlier interval may need a multi-hop path through the earlier version. A question about the later interval may need a path through the later version. But a path that uses the later version as though it held during the earlier interval would have a temporal mismatch. The illustration does not assume any particular entity, dates, or edit.
Where does the question’s own time scope come into the check?

It gives retrieval a constraint to apply to candidate paths. If the question asks about a particular interval, each hop that purports to hold during that interval needs an applicable factual version. A path can then be rejected for that answer if an essential hop only holds outside the required interval. That does not make the hop false; it means it does not support the answer under that time scope.
I’m concerned that rejecting a path might effectively hide the historical version for other questions.

Those should be kept separate. Rejecting a candidate path as support for one temporally scoped answer is not the same as deleting its constituent facts or excluding them from all future retrieval. To avoid suppressing valid historical paths, an earlier version must remain available when a question’s time scope calls for it. The rejection is conditional on the path’s fit to the current question.
Does the presence of an attached patch itself make the earlier version incompatible?

No. The presence of a patch does not, by itself, invalidate a historical version. Compatibility depends on the versions’ validity windows and the temporal demands of the reasoning path. If the earlier version is valid for the period being asked about, a later patch should not displace it merely because the edited entity is encountered.
Could the edited-entity gate still matter if the path reaches that entity only after another hop?

Conceptually, yes. In multi-hop retrieval, the relevance of an edited entity might become apparent partway through a candidate path. At that point, the time-indexed versions associated with the entity would need to be considered in light of the question’s scope. The gate identifies relevance; it does not decide that the patched version applies regardless of time.
What if the intervals overlap only for part of the period named in a question?

That exposes an important ambiguity: an overlap somewhere in the question’s period does not necessarily support an answer about the entire period. Whether partial overlap is sufficient depends on what the question is asking—for example, whether it asks about any point in the period or asserts something throughout it. The current question does not set a rule for resolving such cases, so a compatibility check should not silently treat partial overlap as universal validity.
Would the same caution apply when a question doesn’t state a time clearly?

Yes. If the relevant time cannot be determined from the question and its reasoning context, choosing one factual version as though its interval were unambiguously required could produce an unsupported answer. Interval-indexed retrieval can distinguish versions, but it cannot by itself supply a missing temporal interpretation. How to handle that ambiguity is not specified here.
How should we think about paths that explicitly move from an earlier interval to a later one?

Their hops need not all share a single validity window. Instead, each time-dependent claim would have to be appropriate to the period it describes, and the connection between the periods would have to match what the question asks. Rejecting such a path solely because its windows do not intersect would suppress precisely the kind of historical reasoning you want to preserve.
Then “incompatible” is relative to the temporal claims made by the path, not just a property of two intervals in isolation?

Exactly. Nonoverlapping intervals are incompatible when the path relies on their facts being true at the same required time. They need not be incompatible when the path explicitly concerns different times. The temporal interpretation of the hops and the question determines whether their windows can jointly support the answer.
What would a careful rejection leave intact?

It would leave the individual time-scoped factual versions available and rule out only their invalid use in a particular candidate chain. An earlier version could still support an earlier-time question, while a patch could support a question within its own interval. The point is to prevent a mismatch from propagating into an answer without turning a local rejection into wholesale loss of historical knowledge.
Is this already a settled procedure for interval-indexed retrieval?

No. The node raises a design question, not a completed procedure or a reported result. Comparing a path’s temporal requirements with the validity windows of its hops is a way to frame a possible answer. The exact representation of those requirements, the handling of ambiguous times, and the decision rule for candidate paths remain open.

My hypothesis is that question-time-conditioned interval intersection will reach at least 90% TemporalHop multi-hop accuracy while limiting historical accuracy loss to no more than one percentage point. How does that address the validity-window question?

It proposes using the time required by the question to determine whether the validity intervals along a reasoning path can jointly support an answer. That is intended to rule out paths whose factual versions are incompatible with the question’s temporal scope while leaving historical versions available for questions about their own periods. The ≥90% TemporalHop multi-hop accuracy and ≤1-percentage-point historical accuracy loss are predicted outcomes, not reported results.
Why emphasize that the intersection is conditioned on question time?

Because interval compatibility is not meaningful in isolation from what the question asks. Two factual versions might not support an answer about the same time, yet each could support an answer about its own interval. Conditioning the check on question time is meant to distinguish an inapplicable path from a valid historical one, rather than rejecting historical information simply because its window differs from an edited fact’s window.
Does “interval intersection” mean every window in a multi-hop path must overlap?

Not necessarily as a blanket rule. As we discussed, a question can connect facts from different periods. The hypothesis names question-time-conditioned interval intersection, but it does not specify exactly how the temporal requirements of every kind of hop are represented. Its intended test is whether the windows can support the path under the time relationships the question requires—not whether all historical facts must have been true simultaneously.
So I shouldn’t present a single shared interval across every hop as a settled implementation detail?

Right. That would go beyond the hypothesis and could misstate its purpose for questions that legitimately span periods. You can say that interval intersection is conditioned on question time to check temporal compatibility. The precise mechanics for paths with different temporal relationships remain unspecified here.
How does the historical accuracy limit fit with the TemporalHop target?

They constrain different aspects of the predicted outcome. At least 90% TemporalHop multi-hop accuracy concerns answering the relevant multi-hop questions. A historical accuracy loss of no more than one percentage point concerns preserving answers about historically valid facts. The hypothesis expects both, rather than treating improved performance on time-scoped edited questions as sufficient if historical answers deteriorate.
When I say a loss of at most one percentage point, what is that compared with?

In the stated goal, historical factual accuracy is compared with the unedited model. Read in that context, the hypothesis limits the drop in historical accuracy relative to that baseline to ≤1 percentage point. It does not specify a baseline accuracy value or report a measured drop.
Is the hypothesis also predicting the same limit for unrelated factual accuracy?

Not explicitly. The broader goal includes keeping both historical and unrelated factual accuracy within one percentage point of the unedited model. This particular hypothesis states a ≤1-percentage-point limit for historical accuracy loss, alongside the ≥90% TemporalHop multi-hop accuracy target. It should not be expanded into a separate prediction about unrelated factual accuracy that it does not state.
What is TemporalHop doing in the wording? I want to avoid making claims about it that aren’t given.

TemporalHop names the setting for the hypothesis’s multi-hop accuracy prediction. The wording gives the target—at least 90%—but no further description of its questions, size, construction, or observed results. Calling it the TemporalHop multi-hop accuracy target preserves what is stated without adding those details.
Can you explain the proposed effect on a path with an edited fact in it?

At a conceptual level, the path would have to use a version of that fact whose validity interval fits the time required at that point in the question’s reasoning. The interval check is meant to prevent a version valid for a different period from supporting the answer. This is the behavior the hypothesis expects question-time conditioning to help achieve; it is not evidence that the check has succeeded.
And what about a path using an earlier, still-valid version?

If the question calls for that earlier period, the historical version should remain eligible to support the path. The ≤1-percentage-point historical accuracy loss prediction captures the concern that temporal filtering must not suppress such answers broadly. A path’s rejection for one question time should not make its underlying historical fact unavailable for another.
Does the hypothesis claim that conditioning alone resolves every ambiguity about a question’s time?

No. It predicts performance from question-time-conditioned interval intersection, but it does not say how to interpret every ambiguous time reference. If the question’s temporal scope is unclear, identifying which intervals ought to intersect remains an issue. The hypothesis should not be read as a completed specification for resolving that issue.
What makes this a testable hypothesis rather than just a restatement of the goal?

It identifies a particular proposed mechanism—question-time-conditioned interval intersection—and predicts two measurable outcomes: ≥90% TemporalHop multi-hop accuracy and ≤1 percentage point of historical accuracy loss. Those predicted values could be evaluated. Nothing in the statement says that such an evaluation has occurred or that either result has been achieved.
Would a high TemporalHop score, by itself, establish the whole hypothesis?

No. The hypothesis couples that score with the historical-accuracy limit. Reaching at least 90% TemporalHop multi-hop accuracy would address one prediction; historical accuracy loss would also need to be no more than one percentage point to match the other. Neither outcome is established by the hypothesis’s wording alone.
What if historical accuracy stayed within the limit but the TemporalHop accuracy was below 90%?

That would not match the full prediction either. It would satisfy the historical-loss condition while falling short of the stated TemporalHop multi-hop accuracy threshold. The two conditions are joined in the hypothesis, not offered as alternatives.
Can I describe the central trade-off as rejecting temporally incompatible paths without throwing away valid older ones?

Yes—as the problem the hypothesis is meant to address, not as an accomplished result. Question-time-conditioned interval intersection is hypothesized to support that distinction: reject a path when its validity windows cannot support the answer under the question’s time requirements, while preserving access to historical paths when their windows do fit.
I’d like one compact formulation that keeps the mechanism and both numbers clear.

The hypothesis is that question-time-conditioned interval intersection will yield ≥90% TemporalHop multi-hop accuracy while keeping historical accuracy loss to ≤1 percentage point. Its proposed role is to filter temporally incompatible reasoning paths without suppressing valid historical paths; those performance figures remain predictions, not measured findings.

I plan to construct TemporalHop dated two- and three-hop edits, then compare interval-intersection routing with recency-only routing on edited, historical, and unrelated accuracy. How does that plan bear on the validity-window question?

It sets up a comparison of two ways to route reasoning through dated facts. Interval-intersection routing uses temporal compatibility when considering a multi-hop path; recency-only routing uses recency rather than that compatibility check. Comparing their accuracy on edited, historical, and unrelated questions would help examine whether rejecting incompatible paths can coexist with preserving valid historical ones. This is a plan for a comparison, not a reported outcome.
Why include both two-hop and three-hop edits?

They make the planned comparison about propagation through reasoning chains of two stated lengths, rather than only direct use of an edited fact. A three-hop chain can require the relevant dated fact to remain applicable across more steps than a two-hop chain. The plan specifies both lengths but does not predict a separate result for either one.
What does “dated” contribute to the construction?

It makes time relevant to the edits. Without a temporal qualification, the comparison would say less about whether routing selects facts whose validity windows fit the reasoning being asked for. The plan does not give particular dates or intervals; it calls for dated TemporalHop edits.
Should I describe this as testing whether the newest version is always wrong for historical questions?

No. Recency-only routing is the comparison condition, but the plan does not say it will always give a wrong answer. Its limitation for this question is conceptual: recency by itself does not establish that a fact applies to the time a question requires. The planned accuracy comparison would show how the approaches perform; it has not yet done so.
What distinction does interval-intersection routing make that recency-only routing might not?

Interval-intersection routing considers whether the validity windows needed by a path are compatible with the question’s time requirements. Recency-only routing uses which information is more recent as its routing cue. A recent fact and a temporally applicable fact may coincide, but recency alone does not demonstrate applicability. The comparison is meant to examine the consequence of that distinction, without presuming the results.
I want the historical category to have a clear purpose here.

Historical accuracy speaks directly to the concern that a filter might suppress paths through older facts that remain valid for the periods in question. If the comparison looked only at edited accuracy, it would not reveal that kind of loss. Including historical accuracy lets the planned evaluation consider whether handling dated edits leaves earlier valid answers accessible.
And what does edited accuracy tell us separately?

It concerns answers that need the edited information. That category addresses whether the routing approach actually allows the dated edit to influence relevant reasoning, rather than preserving historical answers by failing to use the edit. Looking at edited and historical accuracy together keeps those two concerns visible.
Why include unrelated accuracy if the immediate question is about time windows?

Unrelated accuracy checks for changes outside the dated edits and the historical paths at issue. It broadens the comparison beyond the paths the routing approaches are intended to affect. The plan names unrelated accuracy as a comparison category; it does not claim that either approach improves or harms it.
So none of the three accuracy categories can simply stand in for the others?

Right. Edited accuracy asks whether relevant changes are used. Historical accuracy asks whether valid earlier answers remain available. Unrelated accuracy asks whether factual answers outside that scope remain accurate. Reporting one category alone would leave the other aspects of the planned comparison unexamined.
Could I say this plan tests the interval-intersection hypothesis?

You can describe it as a planned way to examine interval-intersection routing against recency-only routing. In particular, the dated two- and three-hop edits and the three accuracy categories bear on the question of temporal propagation versus preservation. The plan itself does not report a test result or establish the earlier prediction.
Does the plan say how many edits or questions TemporalHop will contain?

No. It specifies dated two- and three-hop edits in TemporalHop and the two routing approaches and three accuracy categories to compare. It does not specify counts, particular facts, dates, or a detailed scoring protocol. Those should not be presented as settled parts of this plan.
Would it be fair to call recency-only routing a baseline?

Yes, in the limited sense that it is the named comparison approach for interval-intersection routing. Calling it a baseline does not imply a known accuracy, a particular implementation beyond recency-based routing, or a conclusion about which approach performs better.
What would it mean for a valid historical path to be suppressed in this comparison?

Conceptually, the path would be available in principle from historically valid facts but would fail to contribute to an answer about the period when those facts applied. Historical accuracy is the named outcome category that can help reveal whether that concern arises. The plan does not specify a path-level diagnostic or claim that suppression has occurred.
And an incompatible path would be one that uses facts outside the time they need to apply?

That is the central concern. If a reasoning path depends on a factual version holding at a time outside its validity window, it cannot support that temporally scoped answer on that basis. Interval-intersection routing is the approach being compared for handling such compatibility; the plan does not spell out every rule for interpreting a path’s time requirements.
I should avoid assuming every two- or three-hop path needs all its facts to hold at the same instant, correct?

Correct. A path could relate different periods, so the temporal requirements of its hops need to be read in context. The plan names interval-intersection routing, but it does not commit to a blanket rule that every hop in every question must overlap at one instant. That distinction matters if the comparison is meant to address valid historical paths rather than exclude them indiscriminately.
Does constructing dated edits already count as demonstrating that either routing approach works?

No. Construction supplies the material for the planned comparison. The comparative accuracy results would still have to be obtained, and the node provides none. In particular, it does not state which approach is more accurate on edited, historical, or unrelated questions.
How would you state the plan without implying a preferred result?

Construct dated TemporalHop edits requiring two- and three-hop reasoning, and compare interval-intersection routing with recency-only routing on edited, historical, and unrelated accuracy. That states what will be compared and where, while leaving the outcomes open.
The comparison is meant to illuminate both sides of the original question, then: rejecting incompatible paths and not losing valid historical ones?

Yes. The edited and historical accuracy categories make both concerns visible in a comparison of the two routing approaches, while unrelated accuracy checks a further boundary on their effects. Whether interval-intersection routing actually strikes that balance remains to be determined by the planned comparison.

Let’s compare interval-intersection and recency-only routing on TemporalHop v1’s 1,200 held-out questions, measuring edited multi-hop, historical, and unrelated accuracy. What does this activity cover?

It names two routing approaches to compare on the same stated evaluation set: TemporalHop v1’s 1,200 held-out questions. The measurements are edited multi-hop accuracy, historical accuracy, and unrelated accuracy. The activity specifies the comparison and what to measure; it does not provide scores or say which approach performs better.
Why is it important to say “TemporalHop v1” rather than just “TemporalHop” here?

Because TemporalHop v1 is the version specified for this comparison. Naming it preserves the scope of the activity without implying that results from another version are interchangeable. The node does not describe differences between versions.
And the number is 1,200 held-out questions?

Yes: 1,200 held-out questions in TemporalHop v1. That is the stated size of the evaluation set. It does not say how many questions fall under each accuracy category, so the 1,200 should not be turned into separate category counts.
What does held-out establish for this activity?

It identifies the questions as reserved for evaluation rather than as examples used to shape the edits or routing. The term does not, by itself, tell us how the questions were assembled or how the three accuracy measurements are distributed across them.
How does this comparison connect to the question about incompatible validity windows?

Interval-intersection routing is the approach concerned with whether the validity windows used in a reasoning path fit its temporal requirements. Recency-only routing provides a contrasting way of selecting information based on recency. Measuring edited multi-hop and historical accuracy can show how the approaches fare on using applicable edits without losing answers grounded in valid historical facts. The activity has not yet supplied that comparison’s outcome.
Does recency-only routing mean the most recent fact is always false for a historical question?

No. It describes the routing criterion, not a guaranteed error. A recent fact might happen to be relevant to a particular question. The comparison asks how recency-only routing performs against interval-intersection routing across the stated questions, rather than assuming it always fails.
What exactly are we looking for in edited multi-hop accuracy?

That measurement concerns answers requiring edited information through multiple reasoning steps. It is more specific than merely checking whether a direct question can retrieve an edited fact. The activity calls for measuring that accuracy for the routing comparison, but it reports no value for either approach.
Historical accuracy is a separate measurement, correct?

Correct. It addresses whether answers about historically valid facts remain accurate. Keeping it separate from edited multi-hop accuracy matters because a routing approach might use edited facts well while still mishandling earlier periods, or preserve historical answers without adequately propagating applicable edits. Those are possibilities the measurements can distinguish, not findings stated here.
And unrelated accuracy checks something different again?

Yes. It concerns factual answers unrelated to the edits. Including it means the comparison is not limited to whether dated edited and historical facts are handled well; it also considers accuracy outside those affected facts. No change in unrelated accuracy is asserted.
Can I say the 1,200 questions are evenly split among those three measurements?

No. The activity gives the total of 1,200 held-out questions and names three accuracy measurements, but provides no allocation among them. It also does not specify whether their underlying question sets overlap. An even split would be an added assumption.
Does this activity already evaluate the earlier performance hypothesis?

It sets up a comparison relevant to that hypothesis. Edited multi-hop accuracy can be considered against the hypothesized ≥90% TemporalHop target, and historical accuracy bears on the hypothesized ≤1-percentage-point loss. But the activity provides no measured accuracies, so it cannot establish whether either threshold is reached.
Would comparing the two routing approaches by itself tell us the historical loss relative to the unedited model?

Not necessarily. A comparison between interval-intersection and recency-only routing tells us how those approaches compare with each other. A loss stated relative to the unedited model requires that reference accuracy as well. The activity says to measure historical accuracy but does not provide the unedited model’s score or a calculated percentage-point loss.
That distinction seems important: the routing comparison and the preservation threshold don’t use identical reference points.

Right. The two routing approaches are the alternatives named in this activity. The unedited model is the reference for the historical-accuracy preservation requirement discussed earlier.
